extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for writing and evaluating elementary set-theoretic proofs: showing membership, proving subset relations and equality of sets, and basic disproof via counterexamples. Includes worked examples and common proof strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a ∈ {x : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook states the simple test for membership in a set defined by a property: to show a ∈ ({x : P(x)}) one needs only to verify P(a). Example: to show 21 ∈ {x : x∈Z ∧ 7|x} show P(21) is true (21 is divisible by 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show a ∈ {x ∈ S : P(x)}
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that a ∈ S and show that P(a) is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For set-builder notation that includes a restriction, both the domain-membership and the predicate must be checked. The text emphasizes the two-step check (1) a ∈ S, (2) P(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A ⊆ B (Direct approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a ∈ A and deduce that a ∈ B; conclude A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: Suppose a ∈ A. Using definitions and algebraic/logical deductions, show a ∈ B. The direct approach 'usually results in the most straightforward and easy proof' and is the default in many examples. Example proofs demonstrate starting with 'Suppose a ∈ A' and concluding 'Therefore a ∈ B.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A ⊆ B (Contrapositive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a ∉ B and deduce a ∉ A; conclude A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative to the direct method: prove the contrapositive. The text presents this as another option that is sometimes the most expedient. Example outline: Suppose a ∉ B, deduce a ∉ A, thus A ⊆ B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove A ⊆ B (Proof by contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume (a ∈ A) ∧ (a ∉ B) and deduce a contradiction; conclude A ⊆ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes you can also show A ⊆ B by contradiction by assuming an element is in A but not in B and deriving a contradiction. This is presented as an acceptable but occasionally less straightforward method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of method guidance for proving inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct approach is usually simplest; contrapositive may be more expedient in some cases; proof by contradiction is another option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: use the direct approach in most proofs unless a contrapositive or contradiction is clearly simpler. The book indicates it will use the direct approach unless stated otherwise and encourages attention to the outline of the direct approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: To prove set equality A = B
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard two-step procedure: show every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A. The text gives the template: [Prove A ⊆ B.] [Prove B ⊆ A.] Therefore A = B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove equality via chain of equalities/manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform one set expression into the other via a sequence of logically equivalent equalities using definitions and logical equivalences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicable, derive a sequence of equalities (analogous to algebraic manipulation) to transform A into B. The book cautions this approach can be difficult but when it works it can shorten proofs dramatically; demonstrates manipulating set-builder notation and logical equivalences (e.g., using P = P ∧ P) to obtain the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions of set operations explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving membership or inclusions, apply the definitions: e.g., x ∈ A ∩ B means x ∈ A and x ∈ B; (a,b) ∈ A×B means a ∈ A and b ∈ B; X ∈ P(A) means X ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples repeatedly rely on unpacking the definitions of intersection, union, Cartesian product, power set, divisibility, etc. Proofs proceed by invoking these definitions to translate membership statements into simpler component statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case analysis for unions and 'or' conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an assumption yields a disjunction (X ∈ P(A) or X ∈ P(B)), consider separate cases to show the conclusion in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses cases when X ∈ P(A) ∪ P(B): handle Case 1 X ⊆ A and Case 2 X ⊆ B to conclude X ⊆ A ∪ B. It notes you needn't separately handle the overlap because either case covers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating divisibility into existence of integer factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the definition of divisibility: m | a means there exists integer c with a = m·c; use factorization to deduce other divisibility relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples show proving inclusion of divisibility-based sets by writing a = mk and algebraically rearranging to express a as multiple of another integer (e.g., from 18|a deduce 6|a by factoring 18 = 6·3). Use prime factorization where appropriate (e.g., deducing 35|a from 5|a and 7|a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing element of Cartesian product
rubrics_metrics.description: To show (a,b) ∈ A×B, prove a ∈ A and b ∈ B (and conversely use product membership to get component membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show using this to reduce product-membership statements to component-membership facts; used in proofs such as showing A×(B∩C) ⊆ (A×B)∩(A×C) and in arguments leveraging nonemptiness of C to deduce A⊆B from A×C = B×C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving inclusions that follow 'obviously'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subset relations are transparent (e.g., A∩B ⊆ A); these may be used without formal proof unless an exercise requests a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text remarks that obvious set relations need not be proved every time, but recommends mentally verifying them; if a student doesn't see why A∩B ⊆ A but recognizes A ⊆ A∩B is not necessarily true, they should spend more time on the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use known algebraic identities / formulas where helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: When set problems involve numeric expressions (e.g., perfect numbers), apply familiar algebraic results such as formulas for geometric series to compute sums needed in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the proof that certain numbers are perfect, the geometric series sum formula (sum_{k=0}^{n} 2^k = 2^{n+1}-1) is used as a key ingredient. The rubric is to bring in appropriate known results to simplify the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove a statement P
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove the negation ∼P; for universal statements produce a counterexample; for conditionals produce an x with P(x) true and Q(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter on disproof gives explicit procedures: 'How to disprove P: Prove ∼P.' For ∀x∈S, P(x), produce x∈S with ∼P(x). For P(x)⇒Q(x), produce an x with P(x) true and Q(x) false. The counterexample method is presented as simple and utterly convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof strategy guidance / exploratory work
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding truth or falsity of a conjecture, gather evidence and compute examples before attempting a general proof or disproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: evaluate the conjectured formula at several sample inputs (table of f(n) values) to spot patterns or counterexamples; then attempt to prove or produce a counterexample. The text encourages collecting information and trying small cases as part of problem-solving.
